--- title: "Checking a pattern before reporting it" description: "Three checks before a cluster or a gradient goes into a report: whether it comes back in bootstrap samples, whether it is a group or a cut through a gradient, and whether it matches a recorded variable the method never saw." order: 6 categories: [unsupervised, interpretation] --- ## An unsupervised result has no answers to test against k-means and hierarchical clustering return groups for any table, and PCA returns components for any table. A supervised model can be checked against held-out answers; an unsupervised one has no answers to hold out. Three checks take their place, and together they show whether a pattern is worth reporting and what kind of pattern it is. This page puts the two-cluster result from [Clustering with k-means](clustering.qmd) through all three, and then a second split that passes the first check and fails the others. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## The idea ::: {.diagram} ![Three checks before reporting a pattern. Refit on bootstrap samples and see whether the same grouping comes back; look at where the stations sit between the two cluster centres, where real groups leave a gap and a gradient does not; and compare the grouping with a recorded variable that the method was never given.](img/pattern-checks.svg){fig-alt="Three cards side by side with a strip of definitions below. 1 Replication: three small bootstrap samples, each clustered into a blue and an orange group, give the same grouping, captioned the same grouping comes back in every sample. 2 Group or gradient: two small histograms of where stations sit between the two cluster centres, with a dashed boundary line half way; the upper one, labelled groups: a gap, has two humps and almost nothing at the boundary; the lower one, labelled gradient: no gap, is flat from end to end. 3 External check: a column of cluster points, three blue and three orange, each beside a recorded seabed label, hard for every blue point and soft for every orange one, captioned matches a variable the method was never given. The strip reads: bootstrap sample, sites drawn at random with replacement, each with all its stations; ARI, agreement of two groupings, pair by pair, 1 for identical and 0 for chance; recorded variable, measured separately and left out of the analysis."} ::: 1. **Replication.** Refit the clustering on many bootstrap samples and compare each new grouping with the original using the adjusted Rand index (ARI) from [Hierarchical clustering](beyond-k-means.qmd). A real pattern comes back. 2. **Group or gradient.** k-means cuts a gradient as readily as it finds a gap, and a steady gradient is cut in the same place every time, so it comes back too. Where the stations sit between the two centres tells the two apart: groups leave a gap at the boundary, a gradient does not. 3. **An external variable.** Compare the grouping with something recorded separately and left out of the analysis, such as the seabed type. Agreement with a variable the method never saw is the strongest evidence available. ## Worked example ### Sixty bootstrap samples give two answers A **bootstrap sample**, from [Random forests and boosting](../03-supervised-learning/forests-and-boosting.qmd), draws rows at random with replacement. Stations at the same site are more alike than stations from different sites, so here whole sites are drawn, as in [Independence of observations](../06-assumptions-limitations/independence-of-observations.qmd); `group_bootstraps()` in rsample does this. k-means, with the recipe of [Clustering with k-means](clustering.qmd), is refitted on each of 60 samples, and the refitted model assigns every station of the survey to its nearest centre. Each grouping is then compared with the original one, with the recorded seabed, and by how far apart in depth its two clusters sit. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() community <- load_coastal_community() stations <- community |> inner_join(dplyr::select(survey, station_id, site_id, depth_m, substrate), by = "station_id") |> mutate(bottom = if_else(substrate %in% c("rock", "gravel"), "hard", "soft")) taxa_only <- dplyr::select(stations, starts_with("tax")) cluster_workflow <- workflow( recipe(~ ., data = taxa_only) |> step_log(all_numeric_predictors(), offset = 1) |> step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()), k_means(num_clusters = 2) |> set_engine("stats", nstart = 25, iter.max = 100)) fit_clusters <- \(data) fit(cluster_workflow, dplyr::select(data, starts_with("tax"))) assign_clusters <- \(fitted, data) predict(fitted, data)$.pred_cluster set.seed(41) habitat_fit <- fit_clusters(stations) original <- assign_clusters(habitat_fit, stations) set.seed(12) resamples <- group_bootstraps(stations, group = site_id, times = 60) replicates <- map_dfr(resamples$splits, \(split) { assigned <- assign_clusters(fit_clusters(analysis(split)), stations) tibble(agreement = adjustedRandIndex(assigned, original), seabed = adjustedRandIndex(assigned, stations$bottom), depth_gap = abs(diff(tapply(stations$depth_m, assigned, median)))) }) replicates |> mutate(outcome = if_else(agreement > 0.5, "same as original", "different")) |> summarise(samples = n(), `ARI with original` = round(mean(agreement), 2), `ARI with seabed` = round(mean(seabed), 2), `depth between clusters (m)` = round(mean(depth_gap)), .by = outcome) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|outcome | samples| ARI with original| ARI with seabed| depth between clusters (m)| |:----------------|-------:|-----------------:|---------------:|--------------------------:| |same as original | 52| 0.99| 0.91| 30| |different | 8| 0.10| 0.09| 65|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd from sklearn.base import clone from sklearn.cluster import KMeans from sklearn.metrics import adjusted_rand_score from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import FunctionTransformer, StandardScaler from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_community, load_coastal_survey_clean survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() community = load_coastal_community() stations = community.merge( survey[["station_id", "site_id", "depth_m", "substrate"]], on="station_id") stations["bottom"] = np.where(stations["substrate"].isin(["rock", "gravel"]), "hard", "soft") cluster_workflow = Pipeline([ ("log", FunctionTransformer(np.log1p, feature_names_out="one-to-one")), ("normalise", StandardScaler()), ("model", KMeans(n_clusters=2, n_init=25, max_iter=100, random_state=41)), ]) def fit_clusters(data): return clone(cluster_workflow).fit(data.filter(like="tax")) def assign_clusters(fitted, data): return fitted.predict(data.filter(like="tax")) + 1 # scikit-learn has no group bootstrap: draw sites with replacement and # take every station of each site drawn. def site_bootstrap(data, rng): sites = data["site_id"].unique() drawn = rng.choice(sites, size=len(sites), replace=True) return pd.concat([data[data["site_id"] == site] for site in drawn]) habitat_fit = fit_clusters(stations) original = assign_clusters(habitat_fit, stations) rng = np.random.default_rng(12) rows = [] for sample in range(60): assigned = assign_clusters(fit_clusters(site_bootstrap(stations, rng)), stations) medians = stations.groupby(assigned)["depth_m"].median() rows.append({"agreement": adjusted_rand_score(assigned, original), "seabed": adjusted_rand_score(assigned, stations["bottom"]), "depth_gap": abs(medians.iloc[1] - medians.iloc[0])}) replicates = pd.DataFrame(rows) outcome = np.where(replicates["agreement"] > 0.5, "same as original", "different") (replicates.groupby(outcome, sort=False) .agg(samples=("agreement", "size"), ari_original=("agreement", "mean"), ari_seabed=("seabed", "mean"), depth_gap=("depth_gap", "mean")) .round({"ari_original": 2, "ari_seabed": 2, "depth_gap": 0}) .rename(columns={"ari_original": "ARI with original", "ari_seabed": "ARI with seabed", "depth_gap": "depth between clusters (m)"}) .rename_axis("outcome") .reset_index()) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | outcome | samples | ARI with original | ARI with seabed | depth between clusters (m) | |:-----------------|----------:|--------------------:|------------------:|-----------------------------:| | same as original | 52 | 0.99 | 0.91 | 30 | | different | 8 | 0.11 | 0.1 | 65 | ::: ::: ::: In 52 of the 60 samples the original grouping comes back almost exactly, with an average ARI of 0.99: hard bottom against soft. The other 8 give a grouping with almost nothing in common with it. Their clusters barely follow the seabed, with an ARI of 0.09, and sit 65 m apart in median depth against 30 m: they split the survey into shallow and deep. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(replicates, aes(agreement)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.05, boundary = 0, fill = ml_palette[["blue"]], colour = "white") + geom_vline(xintercept = mean(replicates$agreement), linetype = "dashed", colour = ml_palette[["vermilion"]], linewidth = 0.7) + annotate("text", x = mean(replicates$agreement) - 0.02, y = 0.75 * nrow(same), hjust = 1, label = "average", colour = ml_palette[["vermilion"]], size = 3.4) + scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) + labs(x = "ARI with the original grouping", y = "bootstrap samples") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Agreement between each of 60 bootstrap refits and the original grouping. The refits give one of two answers, and nothing in between; the dashed line, the average, falls where no refit landed.](interpreting-patterns_files/figure-html/fig-bootstrap-1.png){#fig-bootstrap fig-alt='Histogram of the adjusted Rand index with the original grouping for 60 bootstrap refits, on an axis from 0 to 1. 8 refits form a short bar near 0.1 at the far left and 52 form a tall bar near 1 at the far right; the range between is empty. A dashed vertical line marks the average, 0.87, in the empty range just left of the tall bar.' width=1300} ::: ::: ::: The average ARI is 0.87, which reads like one stable answer with some noise, but no refit came near it. The data holds two competing two-cluster answers, and the seabed split is the stronger: it came back 52 times out of 60. Report how often each answer came back, not the average. ### A soft-bottom split comes back every time but has no gap Now the soft-bottom stations alone, where the seabed leaves no boundary to find. k-means splits them into two clusters as readily, and the bootstrap check is repeated on them. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} soft <- filter(stations, bottom == "soft") set.seed(41) soft_fit <- fit_clusters(soft) soft_original <- assign_clusters(soft_fit, soft) set.seed(14) soft_resamples <- group_bootstraps(soft, group = site_id, times = 60) soft_agreement <- map_dbl(soft_resamples$splits, \(split) adjustedRandIndex(assign_clusters(fit_clusters(analysis(split)), soft), soft_original)) depths <- tapply(soft$depth_m, soft_original, median) tibble(`median depth, cluster 1 (m)` = round(depths[[1]]), `median depth, cluster 2 (m)` = round(depths[[2]]), `lowest ARI with original` = round(min(soft_agreement), 2), `average ARI with original` = round(mean(soft_agreement), 2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| median depth, cluster 1 (m)| median depth, cluster 2 (m)| lowest ARI with original| average ARI with original| |---------------------------:|---------------------------:|------------------------:|-------------------------:| | 121| 57| 0.69| 0.86|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} soft = stations[stations["bottom"] == "soft"].reset_index(drop=True) soft_fit = fit_clusters(soft) soft_original = assign_clusters(soft_fit, soft) picker = np.random.default_rng(14) soft_agreement = np.array([ adjusted_rand_score( assign_clusters(fit_clusters(site_bootstrap(soft, picker)), soft), soft_original) for sample in range(60) ]) depths = soft.groupby(soft_original)["depth_m"].median() pd.DataFrame([{ "median depth, cluster 1 (m)": round(depths[1]), "median depth, cluster 2 (m)": round(depths[2]), "lowest ARI with original": round(soft_agreement.min(), 2), "average ARI with original": round(soft_agreement.mean(), 2), }]) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | median depth, cluster 1 (m) | median depth, cluster 2 (m) | lowest ARI with original | average ARI with original | |------------------------------:|------------------------------:|---------------------------:|----------------------------:| | 57 | 121 | 0.71 | 0.86 | ::: ::: ::: This split never fails the way the seabed split did: every refit agrees with it at an ARI of 0.69 or more, and none gives a different answer. It divides the soft bottom into a shallow cluster, with a median depth of 57 m, and a deep one at 121 m. By the first check alone, it would be reported as two soft-bottom assemblages. The second check asks whether the two clusters are separated by a gap. Each station gets a position on the straight line from the first cluster centre to the second, 0 at the first and 1 at the second, measured in the logged, standardised counts the clustering used. The boundary between the clusters is half way. Groups leave few stations near the boundary; a gradient leaves as many there as anywhere. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Where each station sits on the line from centre 1 (0) to centre 2 (1). position_between_centres <- function(fitted, data) { scaled <- bake(extract_recipe(fitted), new_data = dplyr::select(data, starts_with("tax"))) |> as.matrix() centres <- extract_fit_engine(fitted)$centers direction <- centres[2, ] - centres[1, ] offset <- sweep(scaled[, colnames(centres)], 2, centres[1, ]) drop(offset %*% direction) / sum(direction^2) } positions <- bind_rows( tibble(split = "All stations, two clusters", position = position_between_centres(habitat_fit, stations)), tibble(split = "Soft bottom only, two clusters", position = position_between_centres(soft_fit, soft), depth_m = soft$depth_m)) positions |> summarise(stations = n(), `share within 0.1 of the boundary` = round(mean(abs(position - 0.5) < 0.1), 3), .by = split) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|split | stations| share within 0.1 of the boundary| |:------------------------------|--------:|--------------------------------:| |All stations, two clusters | 800| 0.021| |Soft bottom only, two clusters | 606| 0.106|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} def position_between_centres(fitted, data): scaled = fitted[:-1].transform(data.filter(like="tax")) centres = fitted["model"].cluster_centers_ direction = centres[1] - centres[0] return (scaled - centres[0]) @ direction / (direction @ direction) positions = pd.concat([ pd.DataFrame({"split": "All stations, two clusters", "position": position_between_centres(habitat_fit, stations)}), pd.DataFrame({"split": "Soft bottom only, two clusters", "position": position_between_centres(soft_fit, soft), "depth_m": soft["depth_m"]}), ]) (positions.groupby("split")["position"] .agg(stations="size", near_boundary=lambda p: round((abs(p - 0.5) < 0.1).mean(), 3)) .rename(columns={"near_boundary": "share within 0.1 of the boundary"}) .reset_index()) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | split | stations | share within 0.1 of the boundary | |:-------------------------------|-----------:|-----------------------------------:| | All stations, two clusters | 800 | 0.021 | | Soft bottom only, two clusters | 606 | 0.106 | ::: ::: ::: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(positions, aes(position)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.05, boundary = 0, fill = ml_palette[["blue"]], colour = "white") + geom_vline(xintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", colour = ml_palette[["vermilion"]], linewidth = 0.7) + facet_wrap(~ split, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") + labs(x = "position between the two cluster centres", y = "stations") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Where each station sits between the two cluster centres, 0 at one centre and 1 at the other; the dashed line is the boundary between the clusters. The seabed split leaves a gap at the boundary; the soft-bottom split cuts through the middle of one broad spread.](interpreting-patterns_files/figure-html/fig-positions-1.png){#fig-positions fig-alt='Two histograms of position between the two cluster centres, from about minus 0.5 to 1.5, with a dashed vertical line at 0.5. Top, all stations: a low, wide hump around 0 and a tall hump around 1, with a dip almost to zero at 0.5, where 2% of stations lie within 0.1 of the boundary. Bottom, soft bottom only: one broad spread from about minus 0.4 to 1.4, with bars running straight across the boundary and no dip, 11% of stations within 0.1 of the boundary.' width=1400} ::: ::: ::: The seabed split has a gap: only 2% of stations lie within 0.1 of its boundary. The soft-bottom split has none: 11% of its stations lie that close, about 5 times as many. The soft-bottom stations run in one continuous line from one centre to the other, and k-means cut the line in the middle. It cuts near the same middle in every bootstrap sample, which is why the split comes back. Depth, which the clustering was never given, shows what the line is. A station's position correlates 0.87 with its depth: the soft-bottom communities change steadily from shallow to deep. The simulation behind the survey agrees, since it gave the 8 soft-bottom taxa depth optima spread from 27 to 153 m with no break between them. ### Only the seabed split matches a recorded category The last check compares each grouping with recorded variables: the seabed, and depth cut into three bands of equal size. For the soft-bottom split, the seabed is sand against mud. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} depth_band <- cut(stations$depth_m, breaks = quantile(stations$depth_m, c(0, 1/3, 2/3, 1)), include.lowest = TRUE) soft_band <- depth_band[stations$bottom == "soft"] external <- tibble( split = c("All stations", "Soft bottom only"), `ARI with recorded seabed` = c(adjustedRandIndex(original, stations$bottom), adjustedRandIndex(soft_original, soft$substrate)), `ARI with depth band` = c(adjustedRandIndex(original, depth_band), adjustedRandIndex(soft_original, soft_band))) external |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|split | ARI with recorded seabed| ARI with depth band| |:----------------|------------------------:|-------------------:| |All stations | 0.92| 0.02| |Soft bottom only | 0.02| 0.38|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} depth_band = pd.qcut(stations["depth_m"], q=3) soft_band = depth_band[(stations["bottom"] == "soft").to_numpy()] external = pd.DataFrame({ "split": ["All stations", "Soft bottom only"], "ARI with recorded seabed": [ adjusted_rand_score(original, stations["bottom"]), adjusted_rand_score(soft_original, soft["substrate"])], "ARI with depth band": [ adjusted_rand_score(original, depth_band), adjusted_rand_score(soft_original, soft_band)], }) external.round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | split | ARI with recorded seabed | ARI with depth band | |:-----------------|---------------------------:|----------------------:| | All stations | 0.92 | 0.02 | | Soft bottom only | 0.02 | 0.38 | ::: ::: ::: The seabed split matches the recorded seabed at an ARI of 0.92 and depth bands at 0.02: from the counts alone, k-means found a category it was never shown. The soft-bottom split matches sand and mud at 0.02 and depth bands at 0.38. Agreement with a recorded **category**, such as the seabed, is evidence of groups. Agreement with a **continuous** variable cut into bands is not: cutting a gradient into two clusters and depth into three bands gives part agreement whether or not groups exist. What it shows is a gradient, and a gradient is a finding too. The three checks together give a result that can be reported: the communities form two groups, hard and soft bottom, found in 52 of 60 bootstrap samples and matching the recorded seabed at an ARI of 0.92; within the soft bottom, composition changes steadily with depth, with no boundary. ## A checked pattern is still a hypothesis The checks show whether a pattern in this survey is worth reporting, not that it holds elsewhere. Treat it as a hypothesis for the next survey, or for a supervised model to test on new data. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - Check three things before reporting a cluster: does it come back in **bootstrap samples**, is it a **group or a cut through a gradient**, and does it match a **recorded variable** the method never saw. - Draw whole sites in the bootstrap when stations at one site are alike. Report how often each answer came back: here 52 of 60 samples gave the seabed split and 8 a depth split, and the average ARI described neither. - **Coming back is not enough.** A split through a steady gradient falls in the same place every time: no bootstrap sample of the soft bottom gave a different answer. - Groups leave a **gap** at the boundary between their centres; a gradient leaves stations all along it. - Agreement with a recorded **category** is evidence of groups. Agreement with a continuous variable cut into bands shows a gradient, which is a finding in its own right. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Replace `group_bootstraps(stations, group = site_id, times = 60)` with `bootstraps(stations, times = 60)`, which draws single stations. How many samples now give the depth split, and why might drawing stations make the result look surer than it is? 2. Repeat the bootstrap check with `num_clusters = 3`. Do the refits still give two competing answers, and what does the third cluster follow?
